title: Someone rebased the branch you were working on
summary: A colleague force-pushed a rebased branch. Your next pull produces a monstrous merge with duplicated commits. Recognise what happened, and recover cleanly with rebase --onto.
mental_model: After a force-push, your local branch and the remote share no recent history — the same changes exist under different shas. Merging glues both copies together; the fix is to replay only your own commits onto the new upstream.
danger: Pulling normally after someone rebases will happily create a merge containing every commit twice. It looks like it worked, and the duplication is discovered days later in review.

steps.title: The colleague's view: something is wrong
steps.why: Run this in the teammate clone. They have one local commit on top of what they fetched — but the branch on the server has been rebuilt, so their base commit no longer exists upstream.
steps.expect: Diverged: commits on both sides, with the same subjects appearing twice.

verify.label: the branch has diverged from its upstream

steps.title: Recognise a rewrite rather than a normal divergence
steps.why: The tell is duplicate subjects with different shas. `git log --left-right` shows both sides carrying 'Add GET endpoint' — that cannot happen from ordinary parallel work.
steps.expect: The same subjects on both sides with different shas — the signature of a force-push.

steps.title: See what the naive fix produces
steps.why: Merging joins the two histories, so every rewritten commit appears twice in the log. The code may even be correct, but the history is now permanently confusing.
steps.expect: Duplicate subjects listed by uniq -d — proof of the double history.

steps.title: Undo that merge
steps.why: `reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` puts the branch back to before the merge. Recognising the problem early is worth far more than any amount of cleverness afterwards.
steps.expect: Back to one copy of each commit.

steps.title: Identify exactly which commits are yours
steps.why: Everything the colleague has that the old upstream did not: one commit. `origin/feature/api@{1}` in the reflog is where their remote-tracking ref pointed before the force-push — the old base.

verify.label: the reflog identifies the pre-rewrite base and your own commit

steps.title: Replay just that commit onto the new upstream
steps.why: `--onto` with the old base as the upstream argument moves only your work. The duplicated commits are simply not in the range, so the result is one clean history with one copy of everything.
steps.expect: Your commit on top of the rewritten branch, and no duplicates at all.

verify.label: exactly one commit sits on top of the rewritten upstream

steps.title: Publish and confirm the branch is sane
steps.why: The push is a fast-forward now, because your branch contains the rewritten upstream. Everyone ends up with one history and one copy of each change.

verify.label: the server has a single clean history
the colleague's branch has no duplicated commits
verify.hint: rebase --onto the new upstream from the old base, do not merge

verify.label: the server ended up with one clean history — five commits, no duplicates
the colleague's branch is back in sync with the server

pitfalls: Duplicate subjects with different shas is the signature of a force-push. Check for it before pulling — `git log --format=%s | sort | uniq -d` takes a second.
`origin/<branch>@{1}` is the reflog of the remote-tracking ref, which survives a force-push and is the cheapest way to find the old base.
`git pull --rebase --fork-point` can work this out automatically in simple cases, but `--onto` with an explicit base is predictable and always correct.
The real prevention is social: never rebase a branch other people are working on without telling them first.
cheatsheet: where the remote ref pointed before the force-push
undo a merge you should not have made
sometimes works this out for you
